L.A. has a surprisingly large gap between city and suburban home prices. Here’s why the difference is so big (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-22/la-homes-still-cost-far-more-than-those-in-suburbs-why-thats-so-surprising)
Home prices in urban Los Angeles are far more expensive than those in the suburbs, despite a shift in homebuyers moving outward from the city, Redfin data show.

But Proposition 37 carries a significant caveat: Any home purchased through the program must be new construction, which could limit its potential reach because of the high cost of building, some critics said.
Also, the proposition does not spell out the terms or interest rates on the loans, which would be worked out if the measure is approved. And some have questioned whether there will be sufficiently robust interest from investors to buy the state-issued bonds that will be used to fund the down payment loans.
The concept of down payment assistance is not new. Cities and states, including California, have long offered such programs to low- and middle-income homeowners, either in the form of loans or grants, and there are reportedly more than 2,700 such programs (https://downpaymentresource.com/professional-resource/down-payment-assistance-continues-to-expand-in-q1-2026-reaching-2679-programs-nationwide/) across the country.
Nevada, Connecticut, Massachusetts and New York all have programs to help homebuyers afford a down payment. Since 2021, New York has dispersed $70 million (https://www.ncsha.org/hfa-news/new-york-state-homes-and-community-renewal-announces-major-milestones-in-expanding-access-to-affordable-homeownership/) in down payment assistance. In Massachusetts, more than $146 million has been doled out in down payment help to homebuyers since 2020.
How the program would work
Under Proposition 37, down payment loans would work like any other, and would carry an interest rate and payback period — all of which would be determined by the California Housing Finance Agency.
To qualify, borrowers would need to have lived in the state for at least a year and earn no more than 200% of the local median income; in Los Angeles County, for example, that equates to a family of four earning no more than $216,200 a year.

Borrowers don’t have to be first-time homebuyers, which is often a requirement of down payment aid programs. But they would need to live in the home.

etween $1 million and $1.5 million and the homes, more importantly, would need to be new construction.
While Proposition 37 has little opposition, and is supported by unions, chambers of commerce and organizations representing builders, the League of Women Voters opposes the ballot measure (https://lwvc.org/ballot-recommendations/), concerned it would saddle residents with too much debt and that the terms of these loans are opaque, the details worked out only after the vote.
New homes only
Only buyers of newly-built homes would be eligible for these loans. That could include existing commercial buildings that had been converted into homes, such as condos or townhomes.
This provision is uncommon as many existing down payment assistance programs don’t strictly limit the type of home someone can buy — only the sale price. Bob Hertzberg, former Senate Majority Leader and the architect of the proposal, said he wanted Proposition 37 to spur new construction.
“The problem is we have to increase supply,” Hertzberg said. The shortage of homes (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2025-09-27/how-bad-is-californias-housing-shortage-it-depends-on-whos-doing-the-counting) in the state is estimated to range anywhere from 840,000 (https://upforgrowth.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/10/2024_Housing-Underproduction-in-the-U.S.-Report_Final-c-1.pdf) to upwards of 3 million. (https://www.mckinsey.com/~/media/mckinsey/industries/public%20and%20social%20sector/our%20insights/closing%20californias%20housing%20gap/closing-californias-housing-gap-full-report.pdf)
Advertisement
By creating more demand for new homes, he said, the hope is that builders will respond en masse.
But some groups are wary of this logic. One analysis (https://voteyeson37.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Prop-37-Homeownership-Analysis-1.pdf), funded by the Proposition 37 campaign, estimated that this program could result in the building of 190,000 homes in the state, although the report’s author said it was “impossible to know” the true number given the various factors that impact housing.
Matthew Lewis, director of communications for California YIMBY, an organization that advocates making it easier and cheaper to build homes, said high prices make it clear that the demand for homes already exists and that Proposition 37 does little to address a bigger issue: the cost of building.

L.A. needs more multifamily housing, but developers say it doesn’t make sense to build apartments in the current market.
Sept. 22, 2026
“In concept, [Proposition 37 is] a great idea,” Lewis said. “The thing we’re concerned about is, California is still way behind on its housing production goals, so there’s the risk of an unintended consequence of instead of having 10 people bidding on a house, now you’ve given a couple folks down payment assistance, and so there’s now 12 people bidding on the same house.”
To drive builders to construct eligible homes, the measure would allow them to opt into a “qualified builder” option. As long as they adhere to price caps, agree to certain labor requirements and fix repairs that arise, they’re protected from lawsuits from buyers concerning defects 10 years after construction of the home.
Homebuilders say even given some relief from litigation, they aren’t sure Proposition 37 would push construction into overdrive.
Advertisement
“There are so many more things the state, city and county could do to help add more supply [of homes],” said Paul Schon, a developer who builds apartments in L.A. County. He said tackling permitting times and red tape involved in building would have a greater impact. “This is minor,” he said.
Interest rates could be a tough sell
Many down payment assistance programs offer interest-free loans to homebuyers, including an existing program run by CalHFA.
But in order to be self-funding, the fixed-rate loans offered through Proposition 37 would carry interest. If passed, the state would issue revenue bonds, selling them to investors and using that money to issue loans to homebuyers. The investors are repaid with the interest paid on the loans.
According to the Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=37&year=2026), CalHFA would decide the total amount of bonds to issue and over what period of time.
Revenue bonds are generally viewed as riskier than other types of government bonds, in part because they’re backed by the promise of revenue from a specific project (https://www.msrb.org/Sources-Repayment) — in this case, payment by individual borrowers. That means interest rates on these loans could be higher than borrowers might like or be able to afford.
Hertzberg said he’s talked to investors who may be willing to buy these bonds at cheaper rates, given the crushing issue the funding is trying to solve. This would keep interest rates down for borrowers. He said he’s appealing to foundations and socially-minded tech leaders.
Advertisement
One of the biggest financial backers of the measure is the political nonprofit Building a Better California, which has been fighting the billionaire’s tax with help from wealthy donors (https://www.latimes.com/business/story/2026-08-12/googles-sergey-brin-spent-102-million-fighting-california-wealth-tax), including Google co-founder Sergey Brin.
Hertzberg, for his part, refused to name any organization or person who may be interested in buying the bonds that would fund this program.

Blog Post · October 7, 2026
How Many Might Actually Use the Down Payment Assistance in Proposition 37?
Eric McGhee (https://www.ppic.org/person/eric-mcghee/)
Subscribe to our blog → (https://www.ppic.org/mailing-list)
Eric McGhee (https://www.ppic.org/person/eric-mcghee/)
Eric McGhee (https://www.ppic.org/person/eric-mcghee/)
California’s homeownership rate is among the lowest in the nation—a full 10 percentage points below the average of all other states—and prices have spiraled beyond what many can afford. Yet for a large number of families, the down payment—not the monthly payment alone—is the wall they cannot climb. Proposition 37, a measure on the fall ballot, would offer a leg up to scale that wall. It would authorize up to $25 billion in revenue bonds to loan as much as 17% of a newly-built home’s purchase price for a down payment. Prop 37 is ambitious and could have a meaningful impact, but the challenges of California’s housing market and current interest rates will limit its reach.
The program has a high income ceiling: 200% of area median income, or in some locations up to $373,000 for a family of four in 2024, the most recent year with Census data. In that year, 91% of renters—the ones most likely to use the program—would have qualified. Qualification ran higher still among groups with the lowest ownership rates: 97% of renters without a high school degree, 93% of Black renters, and 95% of Latino renters.
The home price restriction is also generous. The sales price must fall below 125% of the county’s conforming loan limit—the ceiling on mortgages Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac can purchase, which the Federal Housing Finance Agency sets each year and raises in high-cost counties. That would have covered a home sold for as much as $1.15 million in 2024. While still falling short in some markets, that number would also have beat the statewide median (https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/CAUCSFRCONDOSMSAMID) ($782,000 in December 2024) by roughly 50%.
But income eligibility is not purchasing power, and the math on buying has turned ugly. High prices are now paired with 7% interest rates (https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/24/business/mortgage-rates-7-percent.html) that make a standard 30-year fixed loan with 20% down unaffordable for many. Capping monthly payments at 36% of monthly income (Fannie Mae’s maximum debt-to-income ratio), even an entry-level home at the lowest price range (defined here as the area’s 10 th percentile for new homes) would have been out of reach for 56% of California renters in 2024. Around the state, the median payment for such a home would have been $2,259, and as much as $4,195. One in four homeowners would have been unable to pay it.
Such costs erase much of Prop 37’s ability to address low homeownership rates among certain demographic groups. Among renters without a high school diploma, 71% could not have both qualified for Prop 37 and afforded an entry-level home in their area; three quarters of Black renters would have been in the same position. Latino renters were a partial exception: 39% cleared the bar, largely because they more often lived in lower-cost areas with incomes high enough to buy but still low enough for Prop 37.
Given these limitations, how many people could Prop 37 assist, and how would that compare to the number who might be ready for assistance? We don’t have data on wealth so we can’t say how many would be able to come up with money for a down payment. But setting that aside, if every loan went to a home at the maximum allowable price and drew the full 17% support, the program would have reached roughly 113,000 buyers in 2024—notable, though still far short of the more than one million units California is estimated to need (https://www.ppic.org/publication/housing-in-california/). If the state instead provided 5% of the maximum purchase price it would amount to 409,000 buyers. The full 17% applied to entry-level homes would be 560,000 buyers, and 5% support for entry-level would be 1.8 million. Buyers of cheaper homes will generally need more help, not less, so the 560,000 figure seems a reasonable central estimate that would provide full support for purchases at the low end of the market.
It is worth noting that subsidizing the highest-priced homes reaches farther as a share of potential buyers. The program’s $25 billion would be more than enough to cover the relatively small number of buyers qualifying at the maximum allowable sales price. Conversely, targeting lower prices expands the pool of potential buyers, but beyond what even $25 billion can reach.
Perhaps a better question is whether the program can help California close its ownership gap with the rest of the country. As of 2024, California needed to turn 1.35 million renters into homeowners to match the ownership rate in other states. The maximum 17% support for entry-level homes would have gotten the state about 41% of the way there. Maximum support for the maximum price would have barely made a dent (8%), while the lower five percent support for entry-level homes would have more than closed the gap (136%).
If Prop 37 passes, it will face additional barriers. Many renters would clearly fail to qualify for a conventional mortgage even with the down payment assistance, and many others might not be able to come up with any money for a down payment at all. Moreover, because the money must be spent on newly-built homes, the proposition’s success depends on builders expanding housing inventory.
At the same time, Prop 37’s $25 billion could meaningfully help California close its ownership gap with the rest of the country. The key will be to target, to the extent possible under the rules of the program, homes that are well below the maximum price allowed. Prop 37 might help Californians buy a home, but its dollars must spread across a larger number of lower-spending recipients to have the biggest effect.

While Proposition 37 has little opposition, and is supported by unions, chambers of commerce and organizations representing builders, the League of Women Voters opposes the ballot measure (https://lwvc.org/ballot-recommendations/), concerned it would saddle residents with too much debt and that the terms of these loans are opaque, the details worked out only after the vote.
New homes only
Only buyers of newly-built homes would be eligible for these loans. That could include existing commercial buildings that had been converted into homes, such as condos or townhomes.
This provision is uncommon as many existing down payment assistance programs don’t strictly limit the type of home someone can buy — only the sale price. Bob Hertzberg, former Senate Majority Leader and the architect of the proposal, said he wanted Proposition 37 to spur new construction.
“The problem is we have to increase supply,” Hertzberg said. The shortage of homes (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2025-09-27/how-bad-is-californias-housing-shortage-it-depends-on-whos-doing-the-counting) in the state is estimated to range anywhere from 840,000 (https://upforgrowth.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/10/2024_Housing-Underproduction-in-the-U.S.-Report_Final-c-1.pdf) to upwards of 3 million. (https://www.mckinsey.com/~/media/mckinsey/industries/public%20and%20social%20sector/our%20insights/closing%20californias%20housing%20gap/closing-californias-housing-gap-full-report.pdf)

By creating more demand for new homes, he said, the hope is that builders will respond en masse.
But some groups are wary of this logic. One analysis (https://voteyeson37.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Prop-37-Homeownership-Analysis-1.pdf), funded by the Proposition 37 campaign, estimated that this program could result in the building of 190,000 homes in the state, although the report’s author said it was “impossible to know” the true number given the various factors that impact housing.
Matthew Lewis, director of communications for California YIMBY, an organization that advocates making it easier and cheaper to build homes, said high prices make it clear that the demand for homes already exists and that Proposition 37 does little to address a bigger issue: the cost of building.

“In concept, [Proposition 37 is] a great idea,” Lewis said. “The thing we’re concerned about is, California is still way behind on its housing production goals, so there’s the risk of an unintended consequence of instead of having 10 people bidding on a house, now you’ve given a couple folks down payment assistance, and so there’s now 12 people bidding on the same house.”
To drive builders to construct eligible homes, the measure would allow them to opt into a “qualified builder” option. As long as they adhere to price caps, agree to certain labor requirements and fix repairs that arise, they’re protected from lawsuits from buyers concerning defects 10 years after construction of the home.
Homebuilders say even given some relief from litigation, they aren’t sure Proposition 37 would push construction into overdrive.

“There are so many more things the state, city and county could do to help add more supply [of homes],” said Paul Schon, a developer who builds apartments in L.A. County. He said tackling permitting times and red tape involved in building would have a greater impact. “This is minor,” he said.
Interest rates could be a tough sell
Many down payment assistance programs offer interest-free loans to homebuyers, including an existing program run by CalHFA.
But in order to be self-funding, the fixed-rate loans offered through Proposition 37 would carry interest. If passed, the state would issue revenue bonds, selling them to investors and using that money to issue loans to homebuyers. The investors are repaid with the interest paid on the loans.
According to the Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=37&year=2026), CalHFA would decide the total amount of bonds to issue and over what period of time.
Revenue bonds are generally viewed as riskier than other types of government bonds, in part because they’re backed by the promise of revenue from a specific project (https://www.msrb.org/Sources-Repayment) — in this case, payment by individual borrowers. That means interest rates on these loans could be higher than borrowers might like or be able to afford.
Hertzberg said he’s talked to investors who may be willing to buy these bonds at cheaper rates, given the crushing issue the funding is trying to solve. This would keep interest rates down for borrowers. He said he’s appealing to foundations and socially-minded tech leaders.

One of the biggest financial backers of the measure is the political nonprofit Building a Better California, which has been fighting the billionaire’s tax with help from wealthy donors (https://www.latimes.com/business/story/2026-08-12/googles-sergey-brin-spent-102-million-fighting-california-wealth-tax), including Google co-founder Sergey Brin.
Hertzberg, for his part, refused to name any organization or person who may be interested in buying the bonds that would fund this program.

This provision is uncommon as many existing down payment assistance programs don’t strictly limit the type of home someone can buy — only the sale price. Bob Hertzberg, former Senate Majority Leader and the architect of the proposal, said he wanted Proposition 37 to spur new construction.
“The problem is we have to increase supply,” Hertzberg said. The shortage of homes (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2025-09-27/how-bad-is-californias-housing-shortage-it-depends-on-whos-doing-the-counting) in the state is estimated to range anywhere from 840,000 (https://upforgrowth.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/10/2024_Housing-Underproduction-in-the-U.S.-Report_Final-c-1.pdf) to upwards of 3 million. (https://www.mckinsey.com/~/media/mckinsey/industries/public%20and%20social%20sector/our%20insights/closing%20californias%20housing%20gap/closing-californias-housing-gap-full-report.pdf)
Advertisement
By creating more demand for new homes, he said, the hope is that builders will respond en masse.
But some groups are wary of this logic. One analysis (https://voteyeson37.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Prop-37-Homeownership-Analysis-1.pdf), funded by the Proposition 37 campaign, estimated that this program could result in the building of 190,000 homes in the state, although the report’s author said it was “impossible to know” the true number given the various factors that impact housing.
Matthew Lewis, director of communications for California YIMBY, an organization that advocates making it easier and cheaper to build homes, said high prices make it clear that the demand for homes already exists and that Proposition 37 does little to address a bigger issue: the cost of building.

L.A. needs more multifamily housing, but developers say it doesn’t make sense to build apartments in the current market.
Sept. 22, 2026
“In concept, [Proposition 37 is] a great idea,” Lewis said. “The thing we’re concerned about is, California is still way behind on its housing production goals, so there’s the risk of an unintended consequence of instead of having 10 people bidding on a house, now you’ve given a couple folks down payment assistance, and so there’s now 12 people bidding on the same house.”
To drive builders to construct eligible homes, the measure would allow them to opt into a “qualified builder” option. As long as they adhere to price caps, agree to certain labor requirements and fix repairs that arise, they’re protected from lawsuits from buyers concerning defects 10 years after construction of the home.
Homebuilders say even given some relief from litigation, they aren’t sure Proposition 37 would push construction into overdrive.
Advertisement
“There are so many more things the state, city and county could do to help add more supply [of homes],” said Paul Schon, a developer who builds apartments in L.A. County. He said tackling permitting times and red tape involved in building would have a greater impact. “This is minor,” he said.
Interest rates could be a tough sell
Many down payment assistance programs offer interest-free loans to homebuyers, including an existing program run by CalHFA.
But in order to be self-funding, the fixed-rate loans offered through Proposition 37 would carry interest. If passed, the state would issue revenue bonds, selling them to investors and using that money to issue loans to homebuyers. The investors are repaid with the interest paid on the loans.
According to the Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=37&year=2026), CalHFA would decide the total amount of bonds to issue and over what period of time.
Revenue bonds are generally viewed as riskier than other types of government bonds, in part because they’re backed by the promise of revenue from a specific project (https://www.msrb.org/Sources-Repayment) — in this case, payment by individual borrowers. That means interest rates on these loans could be higher than borrowers might like or be able to afford.
Hertzberg said he’s talked to investors who may be willing to buy these bonds at cheaper rates, given the crushing issue the funding is trying to solve. This would keep interest rates down for borrowers. He said he’s appealing to foundations and socially-minded tech leaders.
Advertisement
One of the biggest financial backers of the measure is the political nonprofit Building a Better California, which has been fighting the billionaire’s tax with help from wealthy donors (https://www.latimes.com/business/story/2026-08-12/googles-sergey-brin-spent-102-million-fighting-california-wealth-tax), including Google co-founder Sergey Brin.
Hertzberg, for his part, refused to name any organization or person who may be interested in buying the bonds that would fund this program.

Blog Post · October 7, 2026
How Many Might Actually Use the Down Payment Assistance in Proposition 37?
Eric McGhee (https://www.ppic.org/person/eric-mcghee/)
Subscribe to our blog → (https://www.ppic.org/mailing-list)
Eric McGhee (https://www.ppic.org/person/eric-mcghee/)
Eric McGhee (https://www.ppic.org/person/eric-mcghee/)
California’s homeownership rate is among the lowest in the nation—a full 10 percentage points below the average of all other states—and prices have spiraled beyond what many can afford. Yet for a large number of families, the down payment—not the monthly payment alone—is the wall they cannot climb. Proposition 37, a measure on the fall ballot, would offer a leg up to scale that wall. It would authorize up to $25 billion in revenue bonds to loan as much as 17% of a newly-built home’s purchase price for a down payment. Prop 37 is ambitious and could have a meaningful impact, but the challenges of California’s housing market and current interest rates will limit its reach.
The program has a high income ceiling: 200% of area median income, or in some locations up to $373,000 for a family of four in 2024, the most recent year with Census data. In that year, 91% of renters—the ones most likely to use the program—would have qualified. Qualification ran higher still among groups with the lowest ownership rates: 97% of renters without a high school degree, 93% of Black renters, and 95% of Latino renters.
The home price restriction is also generous. The sales price must fall below 125% of the county’s conforming loan limit—the ceiling on mortgages Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac can purchase, which the Federal Housing Finance Agency sets each year and raises in high-cost counties. That would have covered a home sold for as much as $1.15 million in 2024. While still falling short in some markets, that number would also have beat the statewide median (https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/CAUCSFRCONDOSMSAMID) ($782,000 in December 2024) by roughly 50%.
But income eligibility is not purchasing power, and the math on buying has turned ugly. High prices are now paired with 7% interest rates (https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/24/business/mortgage-rates-7-percent.html) that make a standard 30-year fixed loan with 20% down unaffordable for many. Capping monthly payments at 36% of monthly income (Fannie Mae’s maximum debt-to-income ratio), even an entry-level home at the lowest price range (defined here as the area’s 10 th percentile for new homes) would have been out of reach for 56% of California renters in 2024. Around the state, the median payment for such a home would have been $2,259, and as much as $4,195. One in four homeowners would have been unable to pay it.
Such costs erase much of Prop 37’s ability to address low homeownership rates among certain demographic groups. Among renters without a high school diploma, 71% could not have both qualified for Prop 37 and afforded an entry-level home in their area; three quarters of Black renters would have been in the same position. Latino renters were a partial exception: 39% cleared the bar, largely because they more often lived in lower-cost areas with incomes high enough to buy but still low enough for Prop 37.
Given these limitations, how many people could Prop 37 assist, and how would that compare to the number who might be ready for assistance? We don’t have data on wealth so we can’t say how many would be able to come up with money for a down payment. But setting that aside, if every loan went to a home at the maximum allowable price and drew the full 17% support, the program would have reached roughly 113,000 buyers in 2024—notable, though still far short of the more than one million units California is estimated to need (https://www.ppic.org/publication/housing-in-california/). If the state instead provided 5% of the maximum purchase price it would amount to 409,000 buyers. The full 17% applied to entry-level homes would be 560,000 buyers, and 5% support for entry-level would be 1.8 million. Buyers of cheaper homes will generally need more help, not less, so the 560,000 figure seems a reasonable central estimate that would provide full support for purchases at the low end of the market.
It is worth noting that subsidizing the highest-priced homes reaches farther as a share of potential buyers. The program’s $25 billion would be more than enough to cover the relatively small number of buyers qualifying at the maximum allowable sales price. Conversely, targeting lower prices expands the pool of potential buyers, but beyond what even $25 billion can reach.
Perhaps a better question is whether the program can help California close its ownership gap with the rest of the country. As of 2024, California needed to turn 1.35 million renters into homeowners to match the ownership rate in other states. The maximum 17% support for entry-level homes would have gotten the state about 41% of the way there. Maximum support for the maximum price would have barely made a dent (8%), while the lower five percent support for entry-level homes would have more than closed the gap (136%).
If Prop 37 passes, it will face additional barriers. Many renters would clearly fail to qualify for a conventional mortgage even with the down payment assistance, and many others might not be able to come up with any money for a down payment at all. Moreover, because the money must be spent on newly-built homes, the proposition’s success depends on builders expanding housing inventory.
At the same time, Prop 37’s $25 billion could meaningfully help California close its ownership gap with the rest of the country. The key will be to target, to the extent possible under the rules of the program, homes that are well below the maximum price allowed. Prop 37 might help Californians buy a home, but its dollars must spread across a larger number of lower-spending recipients to have the biggest effect.

Blog Post · October 7, 2026
How Many Might Actually Use the Down Payment Assistance in Proposition 37?
Eric McGhee (https://www.ppic.org/person/eric-mcghee/)
Subscribe to our blog → (https://www.ppic.org/mailing-list)
Eric McGhee (https://www.ppic.org/person/eric-mcghee/)
Eric McGhee (https://www.ppic.org/person/eric-mcghee/)
California’s homeownership rate is among the lowest in the nation—a full 10 percentage points below the average of all other states—and prices have spiraled beyond what many can afford. Yet for a large number of families, the down payment—not the monthly payment alone—is the wall they cannot climb. Proposition 37, a measure on the fall ballot, would offer a leg up to scale that wall. It would authorize up to $25 billion in revenue bonds to loan as much as 17% of a newly-built home’s purchase price for a down payment. Prop 37 is ambitious and could have a meaningful impact, but the challenges of California’s housing market and current interest rates will limit its reach.
The program has a high income ceiling: 200% of area median income, or in some locations up to $373,000 for a family of four in 2024, the most recent year with Census data. In that year, 91% of renters—the ones most likely to use the program—would have qualified. Qualification ran higher still among groups with the lowest ownership rates: 97% of renters without a high school degree, 93% of Black renters, and 95% of Latino renters.
The home price restriction is also generous. The sales price must fall below 125% of the county’s conforming loan limit—the ceiling on mortgages Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac can purchase, which the Federal Housing Finance Agency sets each year and raises in high-cost counties. That would have covered a home sold for as much as $1.15 million in 2024. While still falling short in some markets, that number would also have beat the statewide median (https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/CAUCSFRCONDOSMSAMID) ($782,000 in December 2024) by roughly 50%.
But income eligibility is not purchasing power, and the math on buying has turned ugly. High prices are now paired with 7% interest rates (https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/24/business/mortgage-rates-7-percent.html) that make a standard 30-year fixed loan with 20% down unaffordable for many. Capping monthly payments at 36% of monthly income (Fannie Mae’s maximum debt-to-income ratio), even an entry-level home at the lowest price range (defined here as the area’s 10 th percentile for new homes) would have been out of reach for 56% of California renters in 2024. Around the state, the median payment for such a home would have been $2,259, and as much as $4,195. One in four homeowners would have been unable to pay it.
Such costs erase much of Prop 37’s ability to address low homeownership rates among certain demographic groups. Among renters without a high school diploma, 71% could not have both qualified for Prop 37 and afforded an entry-level home in their area; three quarters of Black renters would have been in the same position. Latino renters were a partial exception: 39% cleared the bar, largely because they more often lived in lower-cost areas with incomes high enough to buy but still low enough for Prop 37.
Given these limitations, how many people could Prop 37 assist, and how would that compare to the number who might be ready for assistance? We don’t have data on wealth so we can’t say how many would be able to come up with money for a down payment. But setting that aside, if every loan went to a home at the maximum allowable price and drew the full 17% support, the program would have reached roughly 113,000 buyers in 2024—notable, though still far short of the more than one million units California is estimated to need (https://www.ppic.org/publication/housing-in-california/). If the state instead provided 5% of the maximum purchase price it would amount to 409,000 buyers. The full 17% applied to entry-level homes would be 560,000 buyers, and 5% support for entry-level would be 1.8 million. Buyers of cheaper homes will generally need more help, not less, so the 560,000 figure seems a reasonable central estimate that would provide full support for purchases at the low end of the market.
It is worth noting that subsidizing the highest-priced homes reaches farther as a share of potential buyers. The program’s $25 billion would be more than enough to cover the relatively small number of buyers qualifying at the maximum allowable sales price. Conversely, targeting lower prices expands the pool of potential buyers, but beyond what even $25 billion can reach.
Perhaps a better question is whether the program can help California close its ownership gap with the rest of the country. As of 2024, California needed to turn 1.35 million renters into homeowners to match the ownership rate in other states. The maximum 17% support for entry-level homes would have gotten the state about 41% of the way there. Maximum support for the maximum price would have barely made a dent (8%), while the lower five percent support for entry-level homes would have more than closed the gap (136%).
If Prop 37 passes, it will face additional barriers. Many renters would clearly fail to qualify for a conventional mortgage even with the down payment assistance, and many others might not be able to come up with any money for a down payment at all. Moreover, because the money must be spent on newly-built homes, the proposition’s success depends on builders expanding housing inventory.
At the same time, Prop 37’s $25 billion could meaningfully help California close its ownership gap with the rest of the country. The key will be to target, to the extent possible under the rules of the program, homes that are well below the maximum price allowed. Prop 37 might help Californians buy a home, but its dollars must spread across a larger number of lower-spending recipients to have the biggest effect.

etween $1 million and $1.5 million and the homes, more importantly, would need to be new construction.
While Proposition 37 has little opposition, and is supported by unions, chambers of commerce and organizations representing builders, the League of Women Voters opposes the ballot measure (https://lwvc.org/ballot-recommendations/), concerned it would saddle residents with too much debt and that the terms of these loans are opaque, the details worked out only after the vote.
New homes only
Only buyers of newly-built homes would be eligible for these loans. That could include existing commercial buildings that had been converted into homes, such as condos or townhomes.
This provision is uncommon as many existing down payment assistance programs don’t strictly limit the type of home someone can buy — only the sale price. Bob Hertzberg, former Senate Majority Leader and the architect of the proposal, said he wanted Proposition 37 to spur new construction.
“The problem is we have to increase supply,” Hertzberg said. The shortage of homes (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2025-09-27/how-bad-is-californias-housing-shortage-it-depends-on-whos-doing-the-counting) in the state is estimated to range anywhere from 840,000 (https://upforgrowth.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/10/2024_Housing-Underproduction-in-the-U.S.-Report_Final-c-1.pdf) to upwards of 3 million. (https://www.mckinsey.com/~/media/mckinsey/industries/public%20and%20social%20sector/our%20insights/closing%20californias%20housing%20gap/closing-californias-housing-gap-full-report.pdf)
Advertisement
By creating more demand for new homes, he said, the hope is that builders will respond en masse.
But some groups are wary of this logic. One analysis (https://voteyeson37.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Prop-37-Homeownership-Analysis-1.pdf), funded by the Proposition 37 campaign, estimated that this program could result in the building of 190,000 homes in the state, although the report’s author said it was “impossible to know” the true number given the various factors that impact housing.
Matthew Lewis, director of communications for California YIMBY, an organization that advocates making it easier and cheaper to build homes, said high prices make it clear that the demand for homes already exists and that Proposition 37 does little to address a bigger issue: the cost of building.
California (https://www.latimes.com/california)
For Subscribers (https://www.latimes.com/topic/for-la-times-subscribers)
Why L.A. developers aren’t building more apartments, despite epic housing shortage (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-09-22/la-developers-arent-building-more-apartments-despite-epic-housing-shortage)
L.A. needs more multifamily housing, but developers say it doesn’t make sense to build apartments in the current market.
Sept. 22, 2026
“In concept, [Proposition 37 is] a great idea,” Lewis said. “The thing we’re concerned about is, California is still way behind on its housing production goals, so there’s the risk of an unintended consequence of instead of having 10 people bidding on a house, now you’ve given a couple folks down payment assistance, and so there’s now 12 people bidding on the same house.”
To drive builders to construct eligible homes, the measure would allow them to opt into a “qualified builder” option. As long as they adhere to price caps, agree to certain labor requirements and fix repairs that arise, they’re protected from lawsuits from buyers concerning defects 10 years after construction of the home.
Homebuilders say even given some relief from litigation, they aren’t sure Proposition 37 would push construction into overdrive.
Advertisement
“There are so many more things the state, city and county could do to help add more supply [of homes],” said Paul Schon, a developer who builds apartments in L.A. County. He said tackling permitting times and red tape involved in building would have a greater impact. “This is minor,” he said.
Interest rates could be a tough sell
Many down payment assistance programs offer interest-free loans to homebuyers, including an existing program run by CalHFA.
But in order to be self-funding, the fixed-rate loans offered through Proposition 37 would carry interest. If passed, the state would issue revenue bonds, selling them to investors and using that money to issue loans to homebuyers. The investors are repaid with the interest paid on the loans.
According to the Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=37&year=2026), CalHFA would decide the total amount of bonds to issue and over what period of time.
Revenue bonds are generally viewed as riskier than other types of government bonds, in part because they’re backed by the promise of revenue from a specific project (https://www.msrb.org/Sources-Repayment) — in this case, payment by individual borrowers. That means interest rates on these loans could be higher than borrowers might like or be able to afford.
Hertzberg said he’s talked to investors who may be willing to buy these bonds at cheaper rates, given the crushing issue the funding is trying to solve. This would keep interest rates down for borrowers. He said he’s appealing to foundations and socially-minded tech leaders.
Advertisement
One of the biggest financial backers of the measure is the political nonprofit Building a Better California, which has been fighting the billionaire’s tax with help from wealthy donors (https://www.latimes.com/business/story/2026-08-12/googles-sergey-brin-spent-102-million-fighting-california-wealth-tax), including Google co-founder Sergey Brin.
Hertzberg, for his part, refused to name any organization or person who may be interested in buying the bonds that would fund this program.
This article is part of The Times’ equity reporting initiative (https://www.latimes.com/about/pressreleases/story/2023-04-04/l-a-times-launches-equity-reporting-initiative) , funded by the James Irvine Foundation, (https://www.irvine.org/) exploring the challenges facing low-income workers and the efforts being made to address California’s economic divide.

Blog Post · October 7, 2026
How Many Might Actually Use the Down Payment Assistance in Proposition 37?
Eric McGhee (https://www.ppic.org/person/eric-mcghee/)
Subscribe to our blog → (https://www.ppic.org/mailing-list)
Eric McGhee (https://www.ppic.org/person/eric-mcghee/)
Eric McGhee (https://www.ppic.org/person/eric-mcghee/)
California’s homeownership rate is among the lowest in the nation—a full 10 percentage points below the average of all other states—and prices have spiraled beyond what many can afford. Yet for a large number of families, the down payment—not the monthly payment alone—is the wall they cannot climb. Proposition 37, a measure on the fall ballot, would offer a leg up to scale that wall. It would authorize up to $25 billion in revenue bonds to loan as much as 17% of a newly-built home’s purchase price for a down payment. Prop 37 is ambitious and could have a meaningful impact, but the challenges of California’s housing market and current interest rates will limit its reach.
The program has a high income ceiling: 200% of area median income, or in some locations up to $373,000 for a family of four in 2024, the most recent year with Census data. In that year, 91% of renters—the ones most likely to use the program—would have qualified. Qualification ran higher still among groups with the lowest ownership rates: 97% of renters without a high school degree, 93% of Black renters, and 95% of Latino renters.
The home price restriction is also generous. The sales price must fall below 125% of the county’s conforming loan limit—the ceiling on mortgages Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac can purchase, which the Federal Housing Finance Agency sets each year and raises in high-cost counties. That would have covered a home sold for as much as $1.15 million in 2024. While still falling short in some markets, that number would also have beat the statewide median (https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/CAUCSFRCONDOSMSAMID) ($782,000 in December 2024) by roughly 50%.
But income eligibility is not purchasing power, and the math on buying has turned ugly. High prices are now paired with 7% interest rates (https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/24/business/mortgage-rates-7-percent.html) that make a standard 30-year fixed loan with 20% down unaffordable for many. Capping monthly payments at 36% of monthly income (Fannie Mae’s maximum debt-to-income ratio), even an entry-level home at the lowest price range (defined here as the area’s 10 th percentile for new homes) would have been out of reach for 56% of California renters in 2024. Around the state, the median payment for such a home would have been $2,259, and as much as $4,195. One in four homeowners would have been unable to pay it.
Such costs erase much of Prop 37’s ability to address low homeownership rates among certain demographic groups. Among renters without a high school diploma, 71% could not have both qualified for Prop 37 and afforded an entry-level home in their area; three quarters of Black renters would have been in the same position. Latino renters were a partial exception: 39% cleared the bar, largely because they more often lived in lower-cost areas with incomes high enough to buy but still low enough for Prop 37.
Given these limitations, how many people could Prop 37 assist, and how would that compare to the number who might be ready for assistance? We don’t have data on wealth so we can’t say how many would be able to come up with money for a down payment. But setting that aside, if every loan went to a home at the maximum allowable price and drew the full 17% support, the program would have reached roughly 113,000 buyers in 2024—notable, though still far short of the more than one million units California is estimated to need (https://www.ppic.org/publication/housing-in-california/). If the state instead provided 5% of the maximum purchase price it would amount to 409,000 buyers. The full 17% applied to entry-level homes would be 560,000 buyers, and 5% support for entry-level would be 1.8 million. Buyers of cheaper homes will generally need more help, not less, so the 560,000 figure seems a reasonable central estimate that would provide full support for purchases at the low end of the market.
It is worth noting that subsidizing the highest-priced homes reaches farther as a share of potential buyers. The program’s $25 billion would be more than enough to cover the relatively small number of buyers qualifying at the maximum allowable sales price. Conversely, targeting lower prices expands the pool of potential buyers, but beyond what even $25 billion can reach.
Perhaps a better question is whether the program can help California close its ownership gap with the rest of the country. As of 2024, California needed to turn 1.35 million renters into homeowners to match the ownership rate in other states. The maximum 17% support for entry-level homes would have gotten the state about 41% of the way there. Maximum support for the maximum price would have barely made a dent (8%), while the lower five percent support for entry-level homes would have more than closed the gap (136%).
If Prop 37 passes, it will face additional barriers. Many renters would clearly fail to qualify for a conventional mortgage even with the down payment assistance, and many others might not be able to come up with any money for a down payment at all. Moreover, because the money must be spent on newly-built homes, the proposition’s success depends on builders expanding housing inventory.
At the same time, Prop 37’s $25 billion could meaningfully help California close its ownership gap with the rest of the country. The key will be to target, to the extent possible under the rules of the program, homes that are well below the maximum price allowed. Prop 37 might help Californians buy a home, but its dollars must spread across a larger number of lower-spending recipients to have the biggest effect.

I now have a very good understanding. Let me also check:
1. The Sac Bee No editorial (a columnist's op-ed, or is it an editorial board piece? The McClatchy board endorsed Yes; the "Endorsement: No on Proposition 37" in sacbee.com may be a different publication - let me check).
2. League of Women Voters ballot recommendations.
3. Polling on Prop 37.

Let me also consider editorial endorsements: Sacramento Bee/McClatchy (Yes), San Luis Obispo Tribune/East Bay Times/Mercury News editorial boards (No — "Californians can't borrow their way out of our housing crisis" — wait, actually the San Luis Obispo editorial "Reject Props 1 and 37" appears to be an SCNG or Bay Area News Group editorial? The eastbaytimes version suggests Bay Area News Group (BANG) — the East Bay Times, San Jose Mercury News, SLO Tribune are all part of the McClatchy... no wait, Mercury News and East Bay Times are MediaNews/BANG; the SLO Tribune is McClatchy. Hmm, but they have joint editorials sometimes? Actually, the "EDITORIAL: Endorsement: Reject Props. 1 and 37" appeared in sanluisobispo.com and eastbaytimes.com — the Bay Area News Group (BANG) includes East Bay Times, Mercury News, and also SLO Tribune? No — SLO is McClatchy. Hmm, but the sacbee.com article "Endorsement: No on Proposition 37, a risky $25 billion housing experiment" appeared in sacbee.com — that's odd since McClatchy's board endorsed Yes in Prop 37... Wait, actually the McClatchy CA editorial board piece I found first says "recommends a 'Yes' vote on Prop 37" — but then there's another piece titled "Endorsement: No on Proposition 37, a risky $25 billion housing experiment" also on sacbee.com/opinion/us-viewpoints. "us-viewpoints" suggests it's an outside/other viewpoint, perhaps a syndicated editorial from another paper (e.g., the San Diego Union-Tribune). Let me check that piece to see who wrote it.

Also the CalMatters article referenced the San Diego Union-Tribune's endorsement "Props 2, 37 wouldn't yield saner state budgets, more housing" — a No endorsement. So U-T (San Diego) is against. And BANG (Mercury News/East Bay Times) is against. League of Women Voters is against. California YIMBY is skeptical. California Budget & Policy Center skeptical. PPIC notes limitations but says could help meaningfully if targeted at lower-priced homes.

Supporters: Newsom, unions (Carpenters, United Nurses), CTA, California Association of Realtors, CalHFA Treasurer Fiona Ma, Controller Malia Cohen, chambers of commerce, mayors. Also state Republican and Democratic parties? The pro argument says bipartisan support.

Let me look at the SD Union-Tribune editorial and the Sac Bee "No" column, plus maybe the LA Times editorial board position (did they endorse?). Also let me check George Skelton's recommendations (LA Times). And polling (PPIC October 2026 survey likely has Prop 37 numbers).

Let me fetch:
1. https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/us-viewpoints/article317313609.html (No on 37)
2. PPIC October 2026 survey results for Prop 37
3. https://www.sandiegouniontribune.com/2026/10/02/endorsements-props-2-37-wouldnt-yield-saner-state-budgets-more-housing/

Also the Hoover Institution's analysis. Let me do a few searches in parallel.
Let me look at the opposing editorials, polling, and the League of Women Voters' reasons.

NEW! Vote with the League: Answer Key Flyer ( One page flyer with quick list of recommendations )
Below are the League of Women Voters of California’s recommendations ** on the propositions appearing on the November 3, 2026 ballot. We base our recommendations on League positions developed through study and member consensus, and the LWVC Board of Directors carefully reviews each measure before taking a position.
**The LWVC Education Fund has provided an unbiased explanation of each ballot measure to help voters make informed decisions. Visit the link at the end of each recommendation for more about each measure.
Proposition 1
VETERANS & AFFORDABLE HOUSING BONDS
Funding from the 2018 bond for broad affordable housing programs has been spent, and there is a corresponding backlog of affordable housing projects stuck waiting for years for financing. Many families in California continue to endure high housing costs, leading to an increase in homelessness and overcrowding. Public subsidy is necessary to provide safe and stable housing for households at the lowest incomes.
Prop 1 authorizes $10 billion in general obligation bonds for the construction, acquisition, rehabilitation, and preservation of affordable housing and for homeownership programs, plus $1.25 billion, also in general obligation bonds, for veteran mortgage assistance through the CalVet Home Loan Program, expected to be repaid from borrowers’ mortgage payments.
LWVC RECOMMENDS:
Yes on Prop 1 Campaign (https://yesonprop1ca.com/)
Unbiased Explanation: Prop 1 (https://cavotes.org/ballot-measure/2026-prop-1/)
Proposition 2
SAVE FOR CALIFORNIA’S FUTURE ACT
Proposition 2 will allow California to save more money during strong economic years so it can protect schools and other essential services when revenues fall.
California’s budget can change dramatically from one year to the next. The state relies heavily on personal income taxes, including taxes on capital gains. Capital gains are profits people earn when they sell stocks, businesses, real estate, or other investments. These taxes bring in much more money when financial markets are doing well, but that revenue can disappear quickly during an economic downturn.
Prop 2 would help California prepare for those swings. It would allow the state to build a larger rainy-day fund and require it to save more when capital gains revenues are unusually high. That would give California a stronger financial cushion during recessions, natural disasters, public health emergencies, and other difficult periods.
Saving more during good years can help prevent deep cuts to public services during bad years. It can also reduce the need for emergency borrowing and other painful budget actions.
LWVC RECOMMENDS:
Yes on Prop 2 Campaign (https://www.yesonprop2.com/)
Unbiased Explanation: Prop 2 (https://cavotes.org/ballot-measure/2026-prop-2/)
Proposition 3
CHILDREN’S EDUCATION & HEALTH CARE PROTECTION
Proposition 3 would protect funding for schools, health care, and other essential services by keeping California’s current income tax rates on the highest-income 2 percent of taxpayers. Without Prop 3, those rates would fall in 2031, reducing state revenue by an estimated $5 billion to $15 billion each year. Prop 3 would not change anyone’s tax rate today.
About 40 percent of this revenue goes to schools and community colleges. The rest helps fund Medi-Cal and other health and human services, other essential public services, and state budget reserves.
California should not give its highest-income residents a multi-billion-dollar tax cut while schools, health care, and other essential services face serious financial pressure. Prop 3 simply asks the top 2 percent to keep paying the same rates they already pay. The League strongly supports the measure because it protects vital services, helps California weather economic downturns, and keeps the state’s tax system fair.
LWVC RECOMMENDS:
Yes on Prop 3 Campaign (https://www.yesprop3ca.com/)
Unbiased Explanation: Prop 3 (https://cavotes.org/ballot-measure/2026-prop-3/)
Proposition 4
CALIFORNIA FAIR ELECTIONS ACT
Elections should be won, not bought. But in California, personal wealth and access to big donors have become unofficial qualifications for public office. Qualified candidates without wealthy networks are often shut out before voters hear their ideas, while candidates and officeholders spend too much time chasing large checks.
Prop 4 gives Californians a way to change that. It lifts California’s near-total ban on public campaign financing and allows the state and local governments to create voluntary programs. The measure creates no financing program and provides no campaign funding by itself. Each jurisdiction decides whether to adopt a program and how to design and pay for it.
Public financing can make small donations matter more, give candidates without personal fortunes a fairer chance to compete, and let them spend more time listening to voters. By reducing the advantage of incumbents, wealthy donors, and special interests, these programs can make elections more open, competitive, and accountable.
They can also open the door to candidates who better reflect California. Latino, Asian American or Pacific Islander, and Black Californians make up nearly two-thirds of our population but remain vastly underrepresented in local government across much of the state. High campaign costs help keep that barrier in place. When voters can choose candidates who understand their communities and reflect their interests, they have more reason to participate.
Prop 4 protects public money. Candidates must show broad grassroots support and agree to spending limits. Money reserved for education, transportation, or public safety cannot be used. Programs cannot favor incumbents or discriminate by party. Public funds cannot pay legal defense costs or fines or repay a candidate’s personal loan to a campaign. Finally, the measure triples the maximum fine for illegal foreign money in California elections.
Prop 4 gives every California community the freedom to build elections where voters have more power and wealthy donors and special interests have less.
LWVC RECOMMENDS:
Yes on Prop 4 Campaign (https://www.cafairelections.org/)
Unbiased Explanation: Prop 4 (https://cavotes.org/ballot-measure/2026-prop-4/)
Proposition 5
RECALL ELECTION REFORM FOR STATEWIDE OFFICERS
California’s recall gives voters a way to remove a corrupt or failed official. It should never become a back door to state office for a replacement candidate propped up by only a small fraction of voters. However, that is exactly what today’s recall rules allow, since the same ballot that decides removal also determines a replacement based on whoever gets the most votes, even if that’s far short of a majority.
Prop 5 fixes a built-in contradiction in the recall process. Voters are asked to remove an officer by majority vote, then hand that same office to a replacement chosen by whomever gets the most votes, often in a field crowded with dozens of candidates and with no requirement that the winner reach half the vote. That’s a loophole that can easily be exploited. In 2021, had the recall against Governor Newsom succeeded, the leading replacement candidate would have taken office with the support of just 28% of recall voters, a stark illustration of exactly this problem.
Prop 5 restores the recall to its proper purpose: deciding whether an official should remain in office. It shuts down that back door with one clean fix: removing the replacement candidate vote from the recall ballot itself. If a recall succeeds, the vacancy is filled through succession, appointment, or a later election decided by real majority support. These are the same rules used to fill any other vacancy in state government. A recalled officer can still run again later. This is a pro-democracy safeguard too – the choice stays with voters rather than being taken away entirely. What Prop 5 rules out is any return to office through appointment, so a recalled officer can only reclaim the seat by winning a real vote.
This is a matter of basic fairness and majority rule. Prop 5 protects accountability while ending a system that can hand power to a candidate most voters never chose.
LWVC RECOMMENDS:
Yes on Prop 5 Campaign (https://fixtherecall.com/)
Unbiased Explanation: Prop 5 (https://cavotes.org/ballot-measure/2026-prop-5/)
Proposition 37
LOAN PROGRAM FOR MIDDLE-INCOME BUYERS OF NEW HOMES
California must build more homes and make homeownership possible for more families. The League of Women Voters of California has worked toward those goals for decades and supports Prop 1, which would provide $10 billion for affordable housing and homeownership programs and $1.25 billion for veterans’ home loans.
Prop 37 addresses a real barrier: the down payment. But it does so by adding a second mortgage that buyers generally would repay every month.
Prop 37 could help a family buy a home without making it affordable to keep. Buyers generally would repay the Prop 37 loan each month in addition to their first mortgage, property taxes, insurance, repairs, and other costs. Voters would not know the interest rate, loan term, or monthly payment before approving the program.
The program could reinforce racial and economic gaps instead of targeting families facing the greatest barriers . Generations of housing discrimination have left many Black and Latino families with less wealth to draw on, but Prop 37 gives no priority to first-time or first-generation buyers and does not exclude current or former homeowners. Households earning up to twice the area median income could qualify, including some earning more than $300,000 a year, while buyers would still have to provide at least 3 percent of the home price.
The program is not tied to good planning. Assistance could be used only for newly built or newly converted homes, with no requirement that they be near jobs, transit, schools, or services or avoid areas with high transportation, insurance, or natural-hazard costs.
Too much remains undecided. The Legislative Analyst says it is uncertain whether investors would buy the bonds, how the loans would compare in cost with other assistance, or whether the program would result in more homes being built or purchased. The interest rate and repayment terms would be set after the election.
California needs homeownership programs that lower families’ total costs, confront racial barriers to building wealth, and support strong communities. Prop 37 does not meet that test.
LWVC RECOMMENDS:
Unbiased Explanation: Prop 37 (https://cavotes.org/ballot-measure/2026-prop-37/)
Proposition 38
BONDS FOR IMMUNOLOGY MEDICAL RESEARCH
Medical research can save lives, but Prop 38 is the wrong way to fund it. It would authorize $8.4 billion in borrowing for immunology and immunotherapy research and require the state to make $500 million to $600 million in annual debt payments for about 20 years. Those payments would come from the General Fund, which also pays for schools, health care, and other public services.
Borrowing is a poor way to pay for ongoing scientific research. Bonds are best suited to long-lived investments such as buildings and infrastructure. With interest, the Legislative Analyst estimates Prop 38 would cost about 10 percent more, after adjusting for inflation, than paying for the research up front.
Prop 38 would lock billions of dollars into one field of research for years to come. About half of the money would go to a single UC-affiliated research institute and the other half to a grant program, with at least $4.2 billion reserved for cancer, heart disease, and Alzheimer’s research. Scientific opportunities and public health needs change. State funding should be able to respond to those changes rather than locking billions of dollars into one field of research through a ballot measure.
Research royalties are no reason to take on $8.4 billion in debt. When voters approved $3 billion for stem-cell research in 2004, supporters pointed to royalties and millions in new state revenue. By 2022, CIRM reported only $15.6 million in its licensing and royalties fund from royalty payments. Prop 38 again points to research-generated revenue as a way to offset public costs, but the Legislative Analyst says the amount and timing are unknown.
California can support important medical research without committing taxpayers to decades of debt and restricting future choices about where limited public dollars can do the most good.

Advocates of Proposition 2 say they want to make it easier for state lawmakers to beef up the "rainy day" fund to help pay for long-term debt such as pension obligations. But the measure would actually make it easier to raid the fund to use for short-term, non-emergency spending. Above, lawmakers are shown at the state Capitol in June. (AP)
By U T Editorial Board (https://www.sandiegouniontribune.com/author/u-t-editorial-board/)
PUBLISHED: October 2, 2026 at 5:00 AM PDT
Getting your Trinity Audio (https://trinityaudio.ai/) player ready...
State lawmakers — the same ones who have been approving spending plans for years that the Legislative Analyst’s Office says have billions of dollars in structural deficits (https://lao.ca.gov/Publications/Report/5091) despite the California Constitution’s requirement that budgets must be balanced — want you to believe they’re actually conscientious fiscal stewards.
That’s why in 2014, they won approval of a ballot measure that was sold to voters with the claim that it would force the Legislature to set aside 1.5% of general fund revenue to beef up the state’s Budget Stabilization Account — a “rainy day” fund that could be used to pay for specific state debts, starting with unfunded pension and retirement health care obligations.
It would also divert even more money to the fund when capital-gains revenue was surging, a common event in the Golden State due to all the wealthy individuals in Silicon Valley with stock options they can cash in when times are good.
But there was a mammoth loophole: Required contributions to the fund could be reduced or suspended after the governor and a majority of the Legislature declared a “budget emergency.”
That’s exactly what has happened over and over again. “Emergencies” were declared the last three completed fiscal years even though revenue was surging.
Now state lawmakers are back with another sham. Placed directly on the ballot by the Legislature, Proposition 2 would amend the Budget Stabilization Account by lifting the cap on how much could be contributed to it — something voters are being told would strengthen the account.
But that is built on the myth that lawmakers want to contribute more. The measure’s fine print (https://www.ocregister.com/2026/09/26/proposition-2-isnt-about-saving-money-its-another-sacramento-shell-game/) shows its real goal: to make it even easier for the state to avoid paying down long-term unfunded obligations by allowing lawmakers to use new rainy day funds to repay recent “budget borrowing.”
No on Proposition 2. It’s another fake reform meant to make Californians think state lawmakers are actually serious about their responsibilities.
The U-T also opposes Proposition 37 (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_37,_Second_Mortgage_Homebuyer_Program_and_Revenue_Bond_Initiative_(2026)), which is less cynical than Proposition 2 but is equally unlikely to live up to the promises made about it.
The measure authorizes the state to issue up to $25 billion in revenue bonds to fund a middle-class down payment assistance program for purchasing newly constructed homes. Backers say it is structured in a way that ensures private bond investors, not state taxpayers, are on the hook for paying back the borrowing.
Its key provision: Eligible buyers would have to be able to make a 3% cash down payment on a home, but they could secure a fixed-rate second mortgage covering up to 17% of the purchase price. This in theory eliminates the traditional expectation of a 20% down payment.
What it doesn’t do in the slightest is to address the biggest reason California has a massive housing crisis: shelter’s extreme cost. Including condos, the median home price in the state is $775,000 (https://www.noradarealestate.com/blog/california-housing-market/). Median household income is about $99,000, according to a recent Census Bureau report (https://www.census.gov/quickfacts/fact/table/CA/BZA210223). Whether a home purchase involves borrowing 80% or 97% of the sale price, the great majority of families are not going to be able to pay the resulting mortgage or mortgages.
Proposition 37 advocates somehow think that allowing qualified state residents to borrow more is a magic solution to the affordability crisis. But a Zillow calculator shows that with the interest rates available in recent months, a household income of at least $265,000 per year is generally necessary to buy a $775,000 home with a 3% down payment in California. Proposition 37 doesn’t change this daunting picture at all.
There are practical ways that the state could bring down the cost of housing. Leaders could ignore turf-protecting construction trade unions and incentivize use of the sturdy, durable prefabricated homes that now have big market shares in Japan and Great Britain. They could ignore revenue-protecting trial lawyers and fix flawed state rules that incentivize lawsuits against condo builders.

Below are the League of Women Voters of California’s recommendations ** on the propositions appearing on the November 3, 2026 ballot. We base our recommendations on League positions developed through study and member consensus, and the LWVC Board of Directors carefully reviews each measure before taking a position.
**The LWVC Education Fund has provided an unbiased explanation of each ballot measure to help voters make informed decisions. Visit the link at the end of each recommendation for more about each measure.
Proposition 1
VETERANS & AFFORDABLE HOUSING BONDS
Funding from the 2018 bond for broad affordable housing programs has been spent, and there is a corresponding backlog of affordable housing projects stuck waiting for years for financing. Many families in California continue to endure high housing costs, leading to an increase in homelessness and overcrowding. Public subsidy is necessary to provide safe and stable housing for households at the lowest incomes.
Prop 1 authorizes $10 billion in general obligation bonds for the construction, acquisition, rehabilitation, and preservation of affordable housing and for homeownership programs, plus $1.25 billion, also in general obligation bonds, for veteran mortgage assistance through the CalVet Home Loan Program, expected to be repaid from borrowers’ mortgage payments.
LWVC RECOMMENDS:
Yes on Prop 1 Campaign (https://yesonprop1ca.com/)
Unbiased Explanation: Prop 1 (https://cavotes.org/ballot-measure/2026-prop-1/)
Proposition 2
SAVE FOR CALIFORNIA’S FUTURE ACT
Proposition 2 will allow California to save more money during strong economic years so it can protect schools and other essential services when revenues fall.
California’s budget can change dramatically from one year to the next. The state relies heavily on personal income taxes, including taxes on capital gains. Capital gains are profits people earn when they sell stocks, businesses, real estate, or other investments. These taxes bring in much more money when financial markets are doing well, but that revenue can disappear quickly during an economic downturn.
Prop 2 would help California prepare for those swings. It would allow the state to build a larger rainy-day fund and require it to save more when capital gains revenues are unusually high. That would give California a stronger financial cushion during recessions, natural disasters, public health emergencies, and other difficult periods.
Saving more during good years can help prevent deep cuts to public services during bad years. It can also reduce the need for emergency borrowing and other painful budget actions.
LWVC RECOMMENDS:
Yes on Prop 2 Campaign (https://www.yesonprop2.com/)
Unbiased Explanation: Prop 2 (https://cavotes.org/ballot-measure/2026-prop-2/)
Proposition 3
CHILDREN’S EDUCATION & HEALTH CARE PROTECTION
Proposition 3 would protect funding for schools, health care, and other essential services by keeping California’s current income tax rates on the highest-income 2 percent of taxpayers. Without Prop 3, those rates would fall in 2031, reducing state revenue by an estimated $5 billion to $15 billion each year. Prop 3 would not change anyone’s tax rate today.
About 40 percent of this revenue goes to schools and community colleges. The rest helps fund Medi-Cal and other health and human services, other essential public services, and state budget reserves.
California should not give its highest-income residents a multi-billion-dollar tax cut while schools, health care, and other essential services face serious financial pressure. Prop 3 simply asks the top 2 percent to keep paying the same rates they already pay. The League strongly supports the measure because it protects vital services, helps California weather economic downturns, and keeps the state’s tax system fair.
LWVC RECOMMENDS:
Yes on Prop 3 Campaign (https://www.yesprop3ca.com/)
Unbiased Explanation: Prop 3 (https://cavotes.org/ballot-measure/2026-prop-3/)
Proposition 4
CALIFORNIA FAIR ELECTIONS ACT
Elections should be won, not bought. But in California, personal wealth and access to big donors have become unofficial qualifications for public office. Qualified candidates without wealthy networks are often shut out before voters hear their ideas, while candidates and officeholders spend too much time chasing large checks.
Prop 4 gives Californians a way to change that. It lifts California’s near-total ban on public campaign financing and allows the state and local governments to create voluntary programs. The measure creates no financing program and provides no campaign funding by itself. Each jurisdiction decides whether to adopt a program and how to design and pay for it.
Public financing can make small donations matter more, give candidates without personal fortunes a fairer chance to compete, and let them spend more time listening to voters. By reducing the advantage of incumbents, wealthy donors, and special interests, these programs can make elections more open, competitive, and accountable.
They can also open the door to candidates who better reflect California. Latino, Asian American or Pacific Islander, and Black Californians make up nearly two-thirds of our population but remain vastly underrepresented in local government across much of the state. High campaign costs help keep that barrier in place. When voters can choose candidates who understand their communities and reflect their interests, they have more reason to participate.
Prop 4 protects public money. Candidates must show broad grassroots support and agree to spending limits. Money reserved for education, transportation, or public safety cannot be used. Programs cannot favor incumbents or discriminate by party. Public funds cannot pay legal defense costs or fines or repay a candidate’s personal loan to a campaign. Finally, the measure triples the maximum fine for illegal foreign money in California elections.
Prop 4 gives every California community the freedom to build elections where voters have more power and wealthy donors and special interests have less.

Yes on Prop 4 Campaign (https://www.cafairelections.org/)
Unbiased Explanation: Prop 4 (https://cavotes.org/ballot-measure/2026-prop-4/)
Proposition 5
RECALL ELECTION REFORM FOR STATEWIDE OFFICERS
California’s recall gives voters a way to remove a corrupt or failed official. It should never become a back door to state office for a replacement candidate propped up by only a small fraction of voters. However, that is exactly what today’s recall rules allow, since the same ballot that decides removal also determines a replacement based on whoever gets the most votes, even if that’s far short of a majority.
Prop 5 fixes a built-in contradiction in the recall process. Voters are asked to remove an officer by majority vote, then hand that same office to a replacement chosen by whomever gets the most votes, often in a field crowded with dozens of candidates and with no requirement that the winner reach half the vote. That’s a loophole that can easily be exploited. In 2021, had the recall against Governor Newsom succeeded, the leading replacement candidate would have taken office with the support of just 28% of recall voters, a stark illustration of exactly this problem.
Prop 5 restores the recall to its proper purpose: deciding whether an official should remain in office. It shuts down that back door with one clean fix: removing the replacement candidate vote from the recall ballot itself. If a recall succeeds, the vacancy is filled through succession, appointment, or a later election decided by real majority support. These are the same rules used to fill any other vacancy in state government. A recalled officer can still run again later. This is a pro-democracy safeguard too – the choice stays with voters rather than being taken away entirely. What Prop 5 rules out is any return to office through appointment, so a recalled officer can only reclaim the seat by winning a real vote.
This is a matter of basic fairness and majority rule. Prop 5 protects accountability while ending a system that can hand power to a candidate most voters never chose.
LWVC RECOMMENDS:
Yes on Prop 5 Campaign (https://fixtherecall.com/)
Unbiased Explanation: Prop 5 (https://cavotes.org/ballot-measure/2026-prop-5/)
Proposition 37
LOAN PROGRAM FOR MIDDLE-INCOME BUYERS OF NEW HOMES
California must build more homes and make homeownership possible for more families. The League of Women Voters of California has worked toward those goals for decades and supports Prop 1, which would provide $10 billion for affordable housing and homeownership programs and $1.25 billion for veterans’ home loans.
Prop 37 addresses a real barrier: the down payment. But it does so by adding a second mortgage that buyers generally would repay every month.
Prop 37 could help a family buy a home without making it affordable to keep. Buyers generally would repay the Prop 37 loan each month in addition to their first mortgage, property taxes, insurance, repairs, and other costs. Voters would not know the interest rate, loan term, or monthly payment before approving the program.
The program could reinforce racial and economic gaps instead of targeting families facing the greatest barriers . Generations of housing discrimination have left many Black and Latino families with less wealth to draw on, but Prop 37 gives no priority to first-time or first-generation buyers and does not exclude current or former homeowners. Households earning up to twice the area median income could qualify, including some earning more than $300,000 a year, while buyers would still have to provide at least 3 percent of the home price.
The program is not tied to good planning. Assistance could be used only for newly built or newly converted homes, with no requirement that they be near jobs, transit, schools, or services or avoid areas with high transportation, insurance, or natural-hazard costs.
Too much remains undecided. The Legislative Analyst says it is uncertain whether investors would buy the bonds, how the loans would compare in cost with other assistance, or whether the program would result in more homes being built or purchased. The interest rate and repayment terms would be set after the election.
California needs homeownership programs that lower families’ total costs, confront racial barriers to building wealth, and support strong communities. Prop 37 does not meet that test.
